name: Cocktail party effect
statement: A person's own name spoken in a conversation they are ignoring sometimes pulls their attention across, and in the laboratory it does so for about a third of people.
meaning: The phrase covers two claims that are usually run together. The first is that a listener can lock onto one voice in a room full of them, and Cherry showed in 1953 that when the two ears carry different texts almost nothing of the ignored voice survives. The second is that one item does break through, the listener's own name, which Moray reported in 1959. Only the second is the effect people mean when they invoke the cocktail party. It matters because a filter that lets a name through has to have recognised the name, which means the ignored channel was processed for meaning before it was discarded. That is the early against late selection argument, and the own-name finding is the observation both sides have to account for.

origin.where: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
origin.note: Cherry named "the cocktail party problem" in this paper and built the shadowing task, but he ran no name experiment. The own-name finding everyone attaches to the phrase is Moray's, published six years later in the Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.

evidence: Cherry fed one spoken message to each ear and had listeners repeat the right-ear message aloud without omission. He then asked four questions about the left ear: was it speech, what was it about, male or female, what language. Listeners always knew it was speech and nearly always caught the change from a male to a female voice. A steady 400-cycle tone was always noticed. Nobody identified a word or phrase, and nobody could make a definite identification of the language as English. When the ignored message changed from English to German partway through, the listener afterwards said he did not know the language and had assumed it was English. Cherry gives no participant counts for these tests and used no listener more than once. Moray had 12 subjects shadow ten short passages of light fiction at about 130 words a minute. Instructions were hidden in the rejected ear, and half of them were prefixed by the listener's own name. Pooled across the 12, named instructions were heard 20 times out of 39 presentations and unnamed ones 4 times out of 30, t = 3.05, beyond the 1% level. On only four of those 20 occasions did a listener obey and change ears. Conway, Cowan and Bunting ran 40 native English speakers through the shadowing task, 17 men and 23 women. Their 20 high and 20 low spans were not a split of those 40 but were recruited from the upper and lower quartiles of a larger pool. The relevant message ran at 60 words per minute for 5.5 minutes, and the first name went into the irrelevant message after four and after five minutes. Twenty per cent of high spans reported hearing their name, against 65% of low spans, Fisher's exact p = .005. Low spans also made more shadowing errors overall, a mean of 20.88 against 10.00, t(32) = 2.18, p = .04.

replication.headline: A preregistered replication with 80 participants found 29% noticed their own name in the ignored ear, close to the 34.6% Wood and Cowan reported in 1995, and nowhere near the everybody of the popular claim.
replication.detail: Röer and Cowan preregistered the design on OSF and ran 80 German-speaking participants, 59 of them women, mean age 25. The relevant message was 420 words at 60 words per minute in a female voice; the ignored message was a male voice starting 30 seconds later. Names arrived after three, four, five and six minutes. On the questionnaire immediately afterwards, 23 participants, 29%, reported hearing their name. Two reported hearing their yoked partner's name. Shadowing errors confirmed the report: participants who noticed their name made more errors on the word presented at the same time as the name and on the next two words, with Bayes factors of 112.6, above 1000 and above 1000. On the word before the name there was no reliable difference, so the noticing was not just wandering attention. By the third word after, the difference had gone. The working-memory moderator did not survive intact. Comparing top and bottom quartiles of operation span, running span, and the two combined, name detection went 21% against 38%, 28% against 36%, and 21% against 37%, and the Bayesian contingency tests were inconclusive at BF10 = 1.023, 0.582 and 1.018. The online measure did separate the groups: low spans made more shadowing errors around the name, BF10 = 11.68 for the combined score. Röer and Cowan compare their 29% with 33% from Moray, 35% from Wood and Cowan, and 43% from Conway and colleagues averaging the two extreme quartiles. Naveh-Benjamin and colleagues sit higher, with 29 of 50 younger adults, 58%, noticing in their first experiment, and the quartile split of 69% against 33% reproducing Conway's pattern. Their older adults almost never noticed: one of 29, 3%, despite spans matching the low-span young.

study.cite: Röer, J. P., & Cowan, N. (2021). A preregistered replication and extension of the cocktail party phenomenon: One's name captures attention, unexpected words do not. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 47(2), 234-242.

limits: The detection rate is a property of the shadowing task, not of names. Brown and colleagues put 50 people in a multisensory virtual café, had them follow a character at their table while a barista in the background called out orders containing their name, and 94% mentioned unprompted afterwards that they had heard it. Names drew a reliable brain response and a skin-conductance response, but gaze shifts followed roughly 5% of probe words, no more than after control words. So the third of people who notice in headphones is what a hard concurrent repetition task leaves over, and an ordinary room is a different measurement. Direction of the working-memory link flips with instructions, though the evidence for the flip is thinner than it is usually made to sound. Colflesh and Conway told 118 people to shadow one channel and press a key on hearing their name in the other. Of the top quartile of working-memory capacity 66.7% caught it, against 34.5% of the bottom, with capacity a reliable predictor, Wald = 3.85, odds ratio 1.03 per point. Naveh-Benjamin and colleagues ran the same divided-attention design and got 83% against 63% for young adults, but say in the same sentence that the difference was not significant by Fisher's exact test. On their second trial, with the shadowed channel presented visually, high and low spans were level at 79%. Three papers here were not obtained. Both Wood and Cowan papers of 1995 sit on APA PsycNet, which answered every request on 21 September 2026 with an Imperva bot block rather than a paywall notice, and they are described from the abstracts served by PubMed. Röer, Bell and Buchner's 2013 paper is closed at Taylor and Francis, which answers with a Cloudflare challenge, and no open copy appeared in Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, CORE, PubMed Central or web search on the same date. The abstract of the Learning, Memory, and Cognition paper reports 34.6% detection alongside a sample of 34 undergraduates, and those two figures do not divide into each other, so the full paper would be needed to reconcile them. The Röer and Cowan and Naveh-Benjamin papers were read as the author manuscripts deposited in PubMed Central, not as the published versions, which the same block keeps shut.
misreadings: The claim that a name always cuts through is wrong in every laboratory measurement of it. Between 29% and 58% of listeners notice, and the modal finding across sixty years is about a third. Moray's famous 33% is the loosest of those figures. His paper prints no overall detection rate, and the number is a mean frequency, per subject, of hearing one particular hidden instruction. The same table gives 0.80 for the instruction listeners had been warned to expect. Röer and Cowan's reading of it as four of twelve participants is a fair gloss on one row of three. The inverse claim, that noticing means a sharper mind, is also wrong: Conway and colleagues found the opposite, with 65% of low spans noticing against 20% of high spans, and the reading is that high spans are better at shutting the channel out. That inhibition story should be held loosely. Röer and Cowan's preregistered replication found the span difference in the right direction but with Bayes factors around one, meaning the retrospective report on its own settles nothing. Cherry is regularly credited with the name finding, and he never tested names. What he showed is the opposite half of the story, that language, words and meaning in the ignored ear go unreported while voice pitch and a pure tone do not. Semantic salience in general does not reach awareness the way a name does. Röer and Cowan planted semantically anomalous sentence endings in the ignored channel; one participant of 80 noticed, and only when asked directly, and could not say which word it was. It still registers below report, because Brown and colleagues found that semantic violations in the café drew neural and physiological responses of their own.
